name: Dream of the Red Chamber
info: Dream of the Red Chamber, also called The Story of the Stone, is an 18th-century Chinese novel by Cao Xueqin, one of the Four Great Classic Novels, that follows the rise and decline of a wealthy clan in High Qing China.

facts.made: Cao Xueqin, a member of a prominent family that had served the Manchu emperors of the Qing dynasty and whose fortunes had begun to decline; the last 40 chapters of the usual 120-chapter text were edited and published by Gao E and Cheng Weiyuan
facts.form: A novel in written vernacular (baihua), with dialogue in the Beijing Mandarin dialect and much poetry; 80 chapters in the earliest manuscripts, 120 in the Cheng-Gao printed edition, with nearly 40 major characters and over 400 others
facts.where: The Jiaxu manuscript (1754) is in the Shanghai Museum, the Jimao manuscript (1759) in the National Library of China and the Gengchen manuscript (1760) in the library of Peking University; the novel is read in printed editions and translations
facts.known: The Stone and the red dust; Jia Baoyu, Lin Daiyu and Xue Baochai; the Jia clan's decline; the Daguanyuan garden; the Rouge manuscripts and their commentators; Redology; the lost ending and the dispute over the last 40 chapters

t: Cao Xueqin began the novel in the 1740s and left it incomplete at his death in 1763 or 1764; it circulated in hand-copied manuscripts of eighty chapters until Gao E and Cheng Weiyuan printed a 120-chapter edition in 1791 and 1792.

Written in vernacular Chinese with the dialogue in Beijing Mandarin, it follows the fortunes of the Jia clan and the love of Baoyu, Daiyu and Baochai, and is known for its large cast and its female characters.
Scholars still dispute who wrote the last 40 chapters, and a field of study, Redology, grew up around the novel, its manuscripts and its lost ending.
dyk: The earliest manuscripts carry comments in red or black ink by unknown commentators, some of whom may have been members of Cao Xueqin's own family; the most prominent, Zhiyanzhai, revealed much about the original ending, which is now lost.
ev: Cao Xueqin begins composing the novel
The date of the Jiaxu manuscript, now in the Shanghai Museum

Wang Guowei publishes an essay that reads the novel through the philosophy of Arthur Schopenhauer
Hu Shih publishes Studies on A Dream of the Red Chamber, arguing that Gao E wrote the last 40 chapters
David Hawkes publishes the first volume of The Story of the Stone, the first eighty chapters in English for Penguin Classics

Zhou Ruchang and Liu Xinwu produce a new 80-chapter version without the Cheng-Gao emendations

sections.origins:
Dream of the Red Chamber was composed in the 18th century, in the period known as High Qing China. Its author, Cao Xueqin, was a member of a prominent Chinese family that had served the Manchu emperors of the Qing dynasty but whose fortunes had begun to decline. The novel's plot depicts the rise and decline of a family much like Cao's own, and later scholars have stressed its autobiographical side; Cao's clan was similarly raided in real life and suffered a steep decline.

The writing draws on older literature. Its style echoes the plays and novels of the late Ming as well as poetry from earlier periods. Its mythological elements were also inspired by the services Cao was involved in at the Dongyue Temple, whose most venerated gods came from Daoism, Chinese Buddhism, Tibetan Buddhism and shamanic traditions, and the book's spiritual themes and portrayals of mythical figures drew on the stories and oral traditions told about these deities in Beijing. Much of this folklore was already popular during the Yuan dynasty and was retold in various ways in Cao's era. The novel is composed in written vernacular (baihua) rather than Classical Chinese, although Cao was highly proficient in both Chinese poetry and Classical Chinese.
sections.content:
In the novel's frame story, a sentient Stone, left over when the goddess Nüwa mended the heaven aeons ago, wants to enjoy the pleasures of the red dust, the mundane world. It begs a Taoist priest and a Buddhist monk to take it with them and is given the chance to learn from human existence. In the Cheng-Gao versions it is reborn as Jia Baoyu, whence the title The Story of the Stone.

The body of the novel is a detailed, episodic record of life in the two branches of the wealthy, aristocratic Jia clan, the Rongguo House and the Ningguo House, who live in large adjacent compounds in a capital that is not named; the first chapter insists that the dynasty is indeterminate. One of the Jia daughters is made a Royal Consort, and to receive her the family builds the Daguanyuan, a landscaped garden that is the setting for much of the later action. The novel charts the Jias' fall from the height of their prestige, following some thirty main characters and over four hundred minor ones. The central story is the rivalry and friendship among Baoyu, his sickly cousin Lin Daiyu, who shares his love of music and poetry, and another cousin, Xue Baochai, whom he is predestined to marry. The novel also depicts Chinese material culture, including medicine, cuisine, tea culture, festivities, opera, music, architecture and funeral rites, and it makes notable use of poetry.
sections.making:
It is known with certainty that Cao Xueqin began writing the novel in the 1740s. By his death in 1763 or 1764 the first 80 chapters were complete and hand-copied manuscripts of them had begun circulating, first among his friends and a growing circle of aficionados and then on the open market, where they sold for large sums. Cao may also have written drafts of the remaining chapters. The manuscripts circulated under the title Story of a Stone, in slightly varying versions of eighty chapters.

Some 12 independent manuscripts survive, and small differences, rearrangements and possible rewritings make their texts vary a little. They carry comments and annotations in red or black ink from unknown commentators, among them Zhiyanzhai, and are known as the rouge versions (zhiben). They are regarded as the most textually reliable versions. Early manuscripts include the Jiaxu manuscript of 1754, the Jimao manuscript of 1759 and the Gengchen manuscript of 1760. The early chapters are full of prophecies and foreshadowings that hint at how the book would continue, for example that Lin Daiyu will die, that Baoyu and Baochai will marry and that Baoyu will become a monk. A branch of Redology, tanyi xue, is devoted to recovering the lost ending from the commentators' annotations and these hints.
sections.reception:
In the late 19th century the novel's influence was so pervasive that the reformer Liang Qichao attacked it, together with Water Margin, as incitement to robbery and lust and as smothering the introduction of Western-style novels. In 1904 the scholar Wang Guowei wrote an essay that invoked Arthur Schopenhauer, called the novel the tragedy of tragedies, in contrast to the prosperous endings in most earlier drama and fiction, and proclaimed it worthy of being considered the one great masterpiece in the realm of Chinese art.

In the early 20th century Hu Shih, with his students Gu Jiegang and Yu Pingbo, established that Cao Xueqin was the work's author, which reflected a new respect for fiction, and prepared reliable reading texts; lexicographers also used the text to establish the vocabulary of the new standardised language. In the 1920s scholars and devoted readers developed Redology into both a scholarly field and a popular avocation. The young Mao Zedong claimed to have read the novel five times. In 1954 Mao personally criticised Yu Pingbo for failing to emphasise that the novel exposed the decadence of feudal society and the theme of class struggle. The novel initially came under fire during the Cultural Revolution, though it quickly regained its prestige in the following years.
sections.survival:
Until 1791 the novel survived in hand-copied manuscripts. Several early ones are still extant: the Jiaxu manuscript of 1754 is held in the Shanghai Museum, the Jimao manuscript of 1759 in the National Library of China and the Gengchen manuscript of 1760 in the library of Peking University. Beijing Normal University and the Institute of Oriental Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences both also held manuscripts that predate the first printed edition.

In 1791 Gao E and Cheng Weiyuan brought out the first printed edition, the Illustrated Dream of the Red Chamber, and in 1792 a second edition correcting editorial errors. The first 80 chapters were edited from the rouge versions, while the last 40 were newly published; in the 1791 prefaces Cheng claimed to have put together an ending from the author's working manuscripts. This 120-chapter version became the most widely circulated, although the edition contains edits that Cao never authorised. The origin of the last 40 chapters is still debated. Hu Shih argued in 1921 that Gao E wrote them, but the mid-20th-century discovery of a 120-chapter manuscript dating well before 1791 complicated the question; Irene Eber found that it seemed to confirm Cheng and Gao's claim that they only edited a complete manuscript. A 2014 stylistic study argued that two different authors wrote the first 80 and last 40 chapters, and in 2020 Zhang Qingshan said it was unlikely Gao E wrote them.
sections.legacy:
The novel is counted among the Four Great Classic Novels of Chinese literature, and its dialogue in the Beijing Mandarin dialect, which later became the foundation of modern spoken Chinese, made it a resource for reformers who promoted the written vernacular. Its themes and style are evident in many modern Chinese prose works and in the poetry of writers such as An Qi. Critical readings have changed with the times: Marxist interpretation beginning in the New Culture Movement saw it as exposing feudal society's corruption, and since the 1980s critics have embraced its richness and aesthetics in a more multicultural context. Some scholars read its women as challenging the gender norms of Qing society, while others resist seeing Baoyu's traits as gender crossing.

Its translation into English began with extracts by Robert Morrison in 1812 and reached complete versions with A Dream of Red Mansions by Yang Hsien-yi and Gladys Yang (1978 to 1980) and The Story of the Stone by David Hawkes and John Minford (1973 to 1980). It has been translated into Czech, Slovak, Japanese and other languages. More than thirty sequels and continuations have been recorded, some written in the Qing era, and the novel has been adapted for film, television, Cantonese opera, dance drama and, in 2016, an English-language opera by Bright Sheng.

summary: Dream of the Red Chamber is Cao Xueqin's 18th-century novel of the rise and decline of the Jia clan. It circulated as 80-chapter manuscripts until a 120-chapter edition was printed in 1791 and 1792, and the authorship of its last 40 chapters is still debated.
